St. Vladimir of Kiev

St. Vladimir of Kiev

Period

Titles / vocation
Equal-to-the-Apostles · Royal

Introduction

St. Vladimir is commemorated as a prince of Kiev, Equal-to-the-Apostles, and a central figure in the Christianization of Rus. The life relates his family, conversion, baptism, and subsequent religious foundations. His earlier conduct and later change are part of the source's narrative. The profile connects his memory with the broader history of Rus without implying a direct institutional ancestry for every later church.

Read circumstances and sources

Background

Vladimir was a son of Svyatoslav and the grandson of St. Olga of Kiev. His rise amid violent dynastic rivalries centered on Novgorod and Kiev.

[2] Historical editorial biography · Bain, 1911 historical encyclopedia, Vladimir; ancestry, rule, and conversion

Life and notable events

His conversion is connected in the published account with Byzantine Christianity, baptism under the name Basil, marriage to the Byzantine princess Anna, and the baptism of the people of Kiev. These events transformed the public religious life of Rus. The same account contrasts his earlier conduct with later support for churches and organized help for poor and sick people.

[2] Historical editorial biography · Bain, 1911 historical encyclopedia, Vladimir; ancestry, rule, and conversion

The following selection is a 1911 historical encyclopedia account. Its chronology, wording, and historical judgments remain that edition’s; they are not silently harmonized with the modern ecclesiastical life.

[2] Historical editorial biography · Historical edition context

VLADIMIR, ST (c. 956-1015), grand duke of Kiev and of all Russia, was the youngest son of Svyatoslav I. and his mistress Malushka. In 970 he received Great Novgorod as his apanage. On the death of Svyatoslav in 972, a long civil war took place between his sons Yaropolk and Oleg, in which Vladimir was involved. From 977 to 984 he was in Scandinavia, collecting as many of the viking warriors as he could to assist him to recover Novgorod, and on his return marched against Yaropolk. On his way to Kiev he sent ambassadors to Ragvald, prince of Polotsk, to sue for the hand of his daughter Ragnilda. The haughty princess refused to affiance herself to “the son of a bonds woman,” but Vladimir attacked Polotsk, slew Ragvald, and took Ragnilda by force. Subsequently (980) he captured Kiev also, slew Yaropolk by treachery, and was proclaimed prince of all Russia. In 981 he conquered the Chervensk cities, the modern Galicia; in 983 he subdued the heathen Yatvyags, whose territories lay between Lithuania and Poland; in 985 he led a fleet along the central rivers of Russia to conquer the Bulgarians of the Kama, planting numerous fortresses and colonies on his way. At this time Vladimir was a thoroughgoing pagan. He increased the number of the trebishcha, or heathen temples; offered up Christians (Theodore and Ivan, the protomartyrs of the Russian Church) on his altars; had eight hundred concubines, besides numerous wives; and spent his whole leisure in feasting and hunting. He also formed a great council out of his boyars, and set his twelve sons over his subject principalities. In the year 987, as the result of a consultation with his boyars, Vladimir sent envoys to study the religions of the various neighbouring nations whose representatives had been urging him to embrace their respective faiths. The result is amusingly described by the chronicler Nestor. Of the Mussulman Bulgarians of the Volga the envoys reported “there is no gladness among them; only sorrow and a great stench; their religion is not a good one.” In the temples of the Germans they saw “no beauty”; but at Constantinople, where the full festival ritual of the Orthodox Church was set in motion to impress them, they found their ideal. “We no longer knew whether we were in heaven or on earth, nor such beauty, and we know not how to tell of it.” If Vladimir was impressed by this account of his envoys, he was yet more so by the offer of the emperor Basil II. to give him his sister Anna in marriage. In 988 he was baptized at Kherson in the Crimea, taking the Christian name of Basil out of compliment to his imperial brother-in-law; the sacrament was followed by his marriage with the Roman princess.

[2] Historical editorial biography · 1911 historical encyclopedia article; bounded biographical selection

Death and martyrdom

St. Vladimir died at Berestov on July 15, 1015 and was buried in Kiev’s Church of the Tithes. The cited life does not describe his death as martyrdom.

[1] Ecclesiastical saint’s life · Published life; biographical narrative, source anchor “Berestov”

Writings and legacy

He is venerated as Equal-to-the-Apostles for the Christianization associated with his rule. His legacy includes churches, charitable provision, and the development of Christian institutions; it is not a surviving collection of personal theological writings.

[1] Ecclesiastical saint’s life · Published life; biographical narrative, source anchor “helping the poor”
